config.root: You want to change the Constitution. Walk the mechanism design, gate by gate.

start.text: Article V's first gate. What does an amendment need just to be proposed?

majority.text: Not this mechanism — proposals need two-thirds of each chamber (or a convention call by two-thirds of the states, never yet used). Proposing itself is a veto point.

states.text: Proposed. Now ratification: three-fourths of the states — 38 of 50 — must agree.

choices.label: Is there a shortcut around the mechanism?

courts.text: There is only constitutional change by other means: courts and custom doing the work the mechanism makes too costly — which is how 27 amendments stretch across nearly two and a half centuries.

config.why: With House, Senate, president and 38 states as sequential vetoes, the amendment rule is the limiting case of the gridlock interval — stability, deadlock and slow change by design.

activities.anchor: The designers' explicit target was filtering and blocking
activities.caption: true or false — what the 1787 design was for
activities.name: fptFilterJudge

statements.s: The designers' explicit target was filtering and blocking, not maximal democracy.
statements.why: An unelectable-by-design Senate, an electoral college, a supermajority amendment rule — whether the insulation is wisdom or defect is a normative argument; that it is deliberate mechanism design is the formal reading.

statements.s: State legislatures chose senators until the 17th Amendment in 1913.
statements.why: The Senate was unelectable-by-design for its first 125 years.

statements.s: The Constitution requires the Senate's filibuster.
statements.why: Each Senate writes its own rules — the 60-vote world is an accident of housekeeping that hardened into a norm.

statements.s: The design's characteristic outputs are stability, deadlock and slow change.
statements.why: That is what sequencing vetoes produces — the system's signature, not its malfunction.

activities.anchor: The House and Senate are spatial models with furniture
activities.caption: mark the position that wins every majority
activities.name: fptMedianPlace

config.prompt: Voters sit at positions 2, 4 and 9 on one policy dimension. Mark the position that beats both neighbours pairwise:
config.why: The median voter theorem: position 4 beats both 2 and 9 in pairwise comparison — majority rule gravitates to the median legislator's ideal point.

activities.anchor: It is an accident of housekeeping
activities.caption: rebuild how an accident became a 60-vote rule
activities.name: fptFilibusterOrder

config.prompt: How housekeeping hardened into the Senate's defining rule — assemble the sequence:
items: 1806: the Senate's rules revision — after advice attributed to Aaron Burr — deletes the previous-question motion
Unlimited debate becomes possible by accident
The accidental possibility hardens over decades into a norm
Every majority regrets and defends the filibuster in turn
config.why: Rules are chosen parameters — changing a rule changes the game's equilibrium, which is why nothing in the Constitution requires the filibuster.

activities.anchor: The president is a veto player with extra moves
activities.caption: pair each presidential lever with its formal reading
activities.name: fptVetoMatch

config.prompt: The presidency in formal terms — pair each piece with its work:

pairs.right: the threat pulls enacted legislation toward the president's ideal point even when the veto is never cast
priced into every negotiation before the word 'veto' is spoken
each formally an interpretation of existing authority, each contestable in court
each unilateral expansion becomes an inheritance available to the next occupant

config.why: Unilateral action surges under divided government exactly as the model predicts — blocking is an asset even when unused.

activities.anchor: Courts enter spatial models as players
activities.caption: drag the divider — the fifth vote cuts both ways
activities.name: fptCourtCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider — the same median mechanism, two directions:

before.label: protects minorities
before.text: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) used the mechanism precisely because legislatures were gridlocked — court-driven change as the exit route from veto-player deadlock.

after.label: entrenches them
after.text: The same mechanism can lock minorities out — depending on which median is holding the fifth vote.

config.why: Bickel's countermajoritarian difficulty — nine appointed lawyers overriding electorally accountable majorities — made precise by the median-justice theorem.

activities.caption: one line of this convergence briefing is wrong
activities.name: fptConvergeSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's briefing on the median voter theorem is wrong — click it:
lines: The theorem predicts majority rule gravitates to the median legislator's ideal point.
The conditions are strong: one policy dimension, two candidates, full turnout, office-motivated parties.
Primaries select the median of activists, who are measurably more extreme than the general-electorate median.
Full turnout is what real elections deliver, so convergence holds as a description of American politics.
The theorem is a boundary tool, not a description.
config.correction: Differential turnout is one of the assumption failures — real elections break the theorem's conditions routinely, which is why American parties can be far apart while general-election rhetoric sounds centrist.
config.why: Primaries, multi-dimensionality and turnout differences each break convergence — treating the theorem as description instead of boundary is the misconception.

activities.caption: file each effect under its directional pull
activities.name: fptPrimarySort

config.prompt: The primary-era modification — file each effect under its direction:

items.label: nomination contests select the median of activists, measurably more extreme than the general-electorate median
incumbent safety combined with elite divergence
negative partisanship — voting against the other side

config.why: The participation-versus-moderation trade-off, made mechanical: who votes in the nomination decides where the ideal point drifts — polarisation as an institutional artefact, not just a mood.
